catalog_quote: There are 3 degrees of stress: primary or strong, secondary or moderate, and tertiary or weak. Primary and secondary stress are represented by the acute and grave respectively while tertiary stress is unmarked. As in the standard, monosyllables uttered in isolation take primary stress: /báan/ '[I] can [do it]', /srúuəl/ '[It's] easy'; dissyllables of native provenance take primary stress on the ultima: /cənnə́ər/ 'ladder', /ləmbáak/ 'trouble'. The same pattern obtains in dissyllabic compounds: /koon kóon/ 'children', /pləəw tnɔ́l/ 'road, highway'. Polysyllables take primary stress on the ultima, secondary stress on the first syllable: /tòorəsáp/ 'telephone', /wìtsəwɔkɔ́ɔn/ 'engineer'. Within the phrase qualifying elements take primary stress, qualified elements secondary or tertiary stress: /tŋàaj níh/ 'this day = today', /jùp mɛ́ɲ/ 'last night', ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary (strong) stress falls on the last syllable of the word: monosyllables are stressed; native disyllables (minor + major syllable) and disyllabic compounds stress the ultima; polysyllables (loans) stress the ultima with secondary stress on the first syllable. Stress is non-contrastive and predictable from position/syllable type: the stressed syllable is the word-final major syllable, minor syllables (presyllables) carry weak or no stress (confirmed independently by Yodmongkhon 1986 p. 80, Prakorb 1987 pp. 113, 213-214, Ponchanok 2016 p. 97/139).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Jenner: secondary (moderate) stress on the first syllable of polysyllables, e.g. /tòorəsáp/ 'telephone'; three degrees (primary/secondary/tertiary). Yodmongkhon 1986 p. 80 and Prakorb 1987 p. 214 likewise distinguish strong stress (major syllable), weak stress (minor syllable of shape CVN / 'type C') and non-stress (open minor syllables / presyllables).
new_statements.exceptions: Jenner restricts the disyllable rule to words 'of native provenance' and treats polysyllables (mostly loans) separately (still ultima). Prakorb 1987 p. 214 and Yodmongkhon 1986 p. 80 state stress is non-contrastive and need not be marked phonemically; Ponchanok 2016 (Sisaket) says the major syllable is 'usually' the last syllable and stress is non-phonemic. Smalley 1976 p. 48: Northern Khmer is not a tonal language; Jenner p. 61: register is absent in Surin.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolation/citation forms (Jenner p. 66 explicitly: 'monosyllables uttered in isolation take primary stress'). Jenner adds a phrase-level rule on the same page: 'Within the phrase qualifying elements take primary stress, qualified elements secondary or tertiary stress', with four clause-terminal intonation contours described in 2.2 (p. 66-67). The Mahidol theses treat stress at the 'phonological word' rank (one strong-stressed major syllable as nucleus, optional preceding weak/unstressed minor syllable).
new_statements.identity_note: Jenner 1974 describes the Surin (town) dialect from one informant (Aree Somthawin); Yodmongkhon 1986 the Prakhonchai (Buriram) dialect; Prakorb 1987 the Surin dialect; Ponchanok 2016 the Takhian Ram (Sisaket) dialect; Smalley 1976 Surin-area speech. All are sub-dialects of nort2684 with no separate Glottolog codes; they agree on the stress facts. Glottolog also files Chanthaburi and Chachoengsao Khmer (Wayland & Jongman 2001; Wichitkhachee 1996) under nort2684, but those are western-Thailand varieties, not the Surin/Buriram/Sisaket bloc described here.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's final-stress record (Jenner 1974: primary stress on the last syllable): presyllables are the unstressed syllables of disyllables and the foot is minor+major. Adds domain detail (compound = one foot/stress group with first-element vowel shortening; graded reduction paths of unstressed presyllables; numeral 'five' destressed as first member). Placement is implied rather than stated, hence medium confidence; the author defers to Prakorb Phon-ngam 1987 (already in this folder, final stress) for phonological detail.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No dedicated stress section and no sentence of the form 'stress falls on X'. The word is described as a foot = (unstressed minor syllable / presyllable / syllabic nasal) + major syllable; the presyllable of a disyllabic word is the unstressed one and reduces in rapid speech (?VN- > ?əN- > N-, CVN- > CəN- > C-, CrV- > Crə- > C-, CV:- > CV- > Cə- > C-), i.e. stress is on the final (major) syllable of the word. In compounds the whole compound becomes one foot/one stress group and the first element's long vowel is shortened (ko:n prɔh NP vs kon-prɔh compound; /pram/ 'five' loses primary stress and reduces before the numeral it combines with: pram-mɔ:j > pmɔ:j 'six'), again pointing to final prominence within the stress group. The transcription uses ' = stress and a second symbol = 'stress and rising pitch' (p. xviii); in chapters III-IV 'stress (and rising pitch)' is treated as an emphasis/prominence prosody that can be put on any element of a phrase (3.1.3.3 p. 193-194, 3.2.3.3 p. 232-233) - that is phrase-level emphasis, not word stress. The phonology sketch (1.10) states it agrees with Prakorb Phon-ngam 1987 apart from segmental details. No mention of tone (language treated as non-tonal; only intonation arrows).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only the phrase 'primary stress' (p. 54) implies degrees; no secondary-stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Reduction item 11 (p. 54-55): some variant forms 'whose occurrence is not conditioned by loss of stress, but seems to be a matter of colloquialism' (e.g. /pram-pi:l/ > /prəm-pɨl/ 'seven'). Notational caveat: in the compound examples the single stress mark is written at the start of the compound (/'rɔŋ-like:/, /'kon-prɔh/), which literally read would put the mark before the first (shortened) element; given the accompanying statements (first element reduced, presyllables unstressed, /pram/ 'does not carry primary stress' in pram-mɔ:j) I read the mark as flagging 'one stress group', not initial stress, but the thesis does not spell this out.
new_statements.identity_note: Pornpen 1989 describes Northern Khmer as spoken at Ban Koh Tlung, Tambon Burasri, Amphoe Muang, 9 km east of Surin town (author a native speaker, b. Surin 1953; data checked with her 74-year-old mother-in-law from the same village). Same Surin variety as the catalog entry (Jenner 1974's informant was from Surin town); the author states her phonology agrees with Prakorb Phon-ngam 1987 (Surin) except /b d/ not implosive, an extra vowel, and offglides to /ə/.
